prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought optical frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level of uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Round 1 did not weaken the case. No member disputes its scientific merit or maturity, and the objections that were raised concern overlap with earlier prizes, the credit boundary and the category of achievement, not whether the result is secure. The physics rests on a clear sequence. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice, which cancels the light shift so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once, and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock. Ye's group then showed what that idea could deliver, reaching systematic uncertainty near 1e-18 and exposing the many-body and spin-exchange physics that sets the stability, and resolving the gravitational redshift over millimetres. Independent laboratories with Sr, Yb and Hg have reproduced and surpassed these results, and routine international comparisons confirm them. That is the independent confirmation I ask of any candidate, and it comes with a decisive, identifiable contribution from each of the two named people. The citation I propose names both the invention and the development, so that Ye's role is not reduced to a performance improvement and Katori's is not reduced to a technology. It states only what has been demonstrated, namely the 1e-18 level, and does not rely on future gains in constants searches, geodesy or the redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: I take three objections seriously. First, Danielsson, Eriksson and Johansson argue that a discovery about nature, such as a new particle or a new state of matter, is a stronger kind of achievement than a measurement capability, and it is true that no deviation from standard physics has yet been found with lattice clocks. My answer is that the statutes name discoveries and inventions equally, and that this capability has already produced demonstrated physics: the millimetre-scale redshift and many-body clock behaviour are results, not promises. I accept, though, that the case would be stronger with a deviation observed, and that reasonable colleagues weigh this differently. Second, the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes cover the readout and the control of single quantum systems, but not the neutral-atom lattice concept or its realisation at 1e-18, so I consider the overlap real as lineage and not as duplication. Third, the credit boundary is a judgement: Lemonde, Ludlow, Sterr, Gill and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups contributed, and Kroll notes that the invention could be argued as Katori's alone. No member has so far identified a key systematic that was established by a group outside Katori and Ye, and I cannot do so from my own knowledge, so I treat this as an open boundary question and not as a defect in the pair.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth, whom the chair asked whether any key systematic was established outside Katori and Ye, and who is the best placed of us to judge the uncertainty budgets.
responses.response: I want your answer on the record before the ballot, because it decides whether Katori and Ye is a fair boundary. My own reading, as a detector person and not a metrologist, is that the lattice light shift and the magic-wavelength condition are Katori's, the 1e-18 uncertainty budget and the many-body and spin-exchange treatment are Ye's, and the blackbody-radiation shift was refined by several groups including PTB, NIST and SYRTE. If you judge that the blackbody evaluation was an independent decisive step and not a refinement of known physics, I would want the citation to be worded narrowly around the lattice clock so that it does not overreach. If you judge it a refinement, I am content with the pair. I agree with you and with Kroll that the citation should not mention the pending SI redefinition.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson prefers B049 because the discovery of a new class of matter is the centre of the citation, and names B008 as the cleanest fallback.
responses.response: I accept that a new state of matter is the stronger type of achievement in the abstract, and I rely on you and Mehlig for condensed matter. What decides it for me is the attribution. Mehlig himself says he would rather lose the configuration than award it on a distorted record, and Johansson, Lindroth and Olsson all point out that Molenkamp tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and not the Kane-Mele graphene model. A citation worded as 'prediction and observation of the quantum spin Hall effect' would join two results that are not about the same system, and the three-person cap leaves Bernevig, Hughes and the 3D work outside. You call B008 the cleanest fallback; I would say that when the credit is this much cleaner, it should be the first choice and not the fallback. If you and Mehlig can show a citation that states the lineage correctly with exactly Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, I will read it carefully and would then rank B049 as the second configuration.

responses.point: Ulf Danielsson prefers the Higgs discovery (Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee) and says the 2013 prize recognised only the prediction, while conceding that the committee could reasonably find B008 the cleaner prize.
responses.response: I agree with you that the 2013 prize recognised the prediction and that the experimental discovery is a separate and permanent achievement, and I think this is the strongest of the discovery-type cases. As a particle physicist by training I looked again for a principled rule and I still do not have one. Spokespersons at the time of discovery would give Gianotti, Incandela and a third, whereas founding spokespersons give Jenni and Virdee, and any rule fixes a different trio from the same four people. You yourself say that you would rather lose the argument on attribution grounds. I take that as honest, but it is also my reason for not putting the Higgs first: a prize that excludes either Della Negra or one of the others, for a result made by thousands, would invite questions in the committee that I cannot answer with a rule. I keep B056 as my second alternative because the science is not in doubt.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll prefers B008, asks that the citation name invention and realisation at 1e-18, and has disclosed a year in John Hall's laboratory and asked whether the committee should consider recusal.
responses.response: I agree with the wording and have used it. On your disclosure, my view as Chair is that a year in Hall's laboratory as a student, with no collaboration with Katori or Ye, is a field-proximity tie that the committee records and does not by itself require recusal. Your first-place ranking in the opening ballot came before any discussion, and the disclosure is now on the record, so I would let the committee decide this together before the final ballot, and I will not treat your vote as more or less weighty than anyone else's. Your point that a pairing of B008 with a second part is awkward under the three-person cap is also my view, so I am not proposing a two-part configuration.

responses.point: Goran Johansson moved from B012 to B008 and says that if the committee wants a discovery that changed what physicists think possible, B049 or B056 is the stronger type of candidate.
responses.response: Thank you for moving from your own field and for stating your proximity to B012. I agree that B049 and B056 are the stronger type if one counts only the discovery of something new, and that is why I have changed my alternatives to B049 and B056. I think your own description of the clock, a single clear idea that removed the main systematic obstacle and was then understood in every physical detail, is why it is the safer prize to award: it is both a new measurement regime and a result with a clear explanation. I also agree with your suggestion to leave B012 for a later year because of 2025 and because of the Girvin and Huard credit.

uncertainties: Whether any key systematic or technique for the lattice clock (lattice light shift, blackbody radiation, hyperpolarisability, density shift) was established by a group outside Katori and Ye; I rely on Lindroth for this and could not answer it from my own field.
Whether the committee reads the 2005 and 2012 prizes as overlap that weakens the novelty of a lattice clock prize, or as groundwork that it completes.
Whether the committee prefers a new measurement capability over a discovery about nature when no deviation from standard physics has yet been seen.

Whether a defensible rule exists for a three-person Higgs prize, and whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D topological insulator problems can be solved in a citation; I have no expertise in the second and rely on Eriksson, Mehlig and Johansson.
How the committee handles Kroll's disclosed tie to the Hall group, and whether the committee wishes to record a recusal decision before the final ballot.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1. I am a member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and am based at KTH; none of these has a connection to Katori, Ye, the optical lattice clock or the alternatives B049 and B056, and I disclose no personal or institutional tie to any credited name. IceCube (B042), which I ranked first in my opening ballot, is no longer in my configuration or my alternatives; my Fermi-LAT field-proximity tie to B042 therefore does not affect my position. As Chair I note Kroll's disclosure and Johansson's and Olsson's proposed recusals (B012 and B009) and propose that the committee settle them openly before the final ballot.
